To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“Switching to ATV/r from LPV/r significantly improves insulin sensitivity, reduces visceral fat, and improves dyslipidemia in HIV-infected individuals with evidence of insulin resistance and dyslipidemia.”

switching from lopanavir/ritanovir (LPV/r; Kaletra) to atazavair/ritanovair (ATV/r; Reyataz) significantly increases glucose uptake in muscle, decreases abdominal fat, improves lipid parameters and decreases fasting glucose.

switching from LPV/r-containing to ATV/r-containing ART significantly increases muscle glucose uptake and decreases abdominal visceral adiposity, improves lipid parameters and decreases fasting glucose in HIV-infected individuals with evidence of hyperlipidemia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effect of switching from loperamide to atazanovir on muscle glucose uptake.
the effects of switching to ATV/r on glucose uptake by muscle and visceral fat in individuals with HIV infection who have evidence of insulin resistance and/or dyslipidaemia.
the study of the influence of the HIV virus and its treatment on the body.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of atazanavir is a good option for the treatment of HIV patients.
the study results suggest that switching to ATV/r from LPV/r may improve metabolic abnormalities in patients on antiretroviral therapy.

switching from LPV/r (a protease inhibitor) to ATV/r (a proteas inhibitor) improves metabolic abnormalities and is a viable option in HIV-infected individuals who are on a proteas inhibitor and are at risk for cardiovascular complications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

switching from lopinvir/ritonavir (lopinavir and ritonavir) to atazavir/ritonavir significantly increased muscle glucose uptake, decreased fasting glucose, visceral adipose tissue and triglycerides, and decreased total cholesterol over 6 months.
the switch to ATV/r improves the metabolic profile in patients who are on a regimen containing lopinavir.
switching to ATV/r from LPV/r is a reasonable strategy to reduce the risk of insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and cardiovascular disease in HIV-infected individuals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
switching to atazanavoir/ritonavir from lopinavoir/ritonavoir is a good option for patients with HIV who have hyperinsulinemia, hyperlipidemia, or both.
switching to ATV/r is an effective strategy to reduce insulin resistance, visceral adiposity, and lipid abnormalities in patients who are already receiving LPV/r.
switching to atazanavair from a protease inhibitor that has more adverse effects on lipids and glucose metabolism can be a good option for HIV-positive patients with metabolic complications.
